questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the test for whether an NFR elicitation and documentation effort was actually worthwhile?
options: Whether the NFR document was approved at a governance checkpoint
Whether the NFR document is longer than ten pages
Whether the NFR was written using the exact metric/target/condition format
Whether you can point to a specific design decision and say which NFR caused it to be made differently than the default
questions.explain: A technically well-written NFR that never actually changes a design decision hasn't done its job. The real test is whether a specific decision can be traced back to a specific NFR causing it to differ from what would otherwise have been built.

questions.q: What are the three parts of this lesson's trace pattern for connecting an NFR to a real decision?
options: Metric, target, condition
Requirement, implication, decision
Confidentiality, integrity, availability
Owner, steward, custodian
questions.explain: The trace pattern explicitly states the requirement, what it implies architecturally, and the specific decision made because of that implication — including what alternative was rejected and why.

questions.q: In the automation-design worked example, why was the notification callout moved off the synchronous record-triggered Flow?
options: Because synchronous Flows cannot make external callouts at all
Because asynchronous processing is always required by Salesforce governor limits
Because a slow or unavailable external endpoint running inline would directly threaten the 2-second, 95th-percentile performance target during exactly the spike scenario the NFR called out
Because the Case object does not support record-triggered Flows
questions.explain: Any synchronous work competing for the smaller sync CPU budget, especially an external callout that might be slow or unavailable, directly threatens a tight performance target — moving it asynchronous removes that risk from the user-facing transaction.

questions.q: In the integration-design worked example, why was upserting against an External ID field chosen over always inserting and relying on a later cleanup job?
options: Because always inserting leaves duplicate data live and possibly acted on by other automation for however long the cleanup job takes, while upserting against an External ID makes the write idempotent from the start
Because upsert is the only DML operation available in Apex
Because External ID fields are required on every Salesforce object by default
Because the cleanup job approach is forbidden by Salesforce governor limits
questions.explain: The reliability NFR required tolerating retried confirmations without creating duplicates. Upserting against an External ID produces the same end state regardless of how many times the operation runs, while a later cleanup job leaves duplicates live (and potentially acted on) in the meantime.

questions.q: What signal does this lesson suggest if you can't identify any design option you explicitly rejected while writing an NFR's trace?
options: That the NFR is unnecessary and should be deleted
That the requirement should be escalated immediately to legal and compliance
That the NFR belongs in a different chapter of the course
That the NFR may not have actually changed anything yet, and the decision should be revisited until it does
questions.explain: If no rejected alternative exists, it suggests the NFR was written but never actually used to steer the design away from its default path — exactly the failure mode this lesson's trace pattern is meant to catch.
